title: Diffusion and particle movement
keyIdea: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It happens because particles in liquids and gases move randomly all the time, not because they aim for the empty space: more particles start where it is crowded, so more cross out of it than back in. When the particles are evenly spread they keep moving, but the crossings balance and there is no net movement. Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids, and faster when it is warmer.

kid: Open a bottle of perfume at one end of a still room and, a little later, people at the other end smell it. Nobody fans it. The perfume spreads by diffusion. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from where there are lots of them to where there are few. Scientists say from high concentration to low concentration.

Particles in a gas or a liquid are always moving in random directions. They bump into each other and change direction all the time. One particle does not know where the empty space is. It just zigzags. But more particles start on the crowded side, so more of them happen to cross out of it than cross back.
In the end the particles are spread evenly. They do not stop moving. Just as many cross each way, so there is no net movement. The concentration stays the same everywhere.

Diffusion is faster when it is warmer, because the particles move faster. It is much faster in a gas than in a liquid. Gas particles are far apart and travel a long way between bumps. Liquid particles are packed close, so they bump all the time and spread slowly.
adult: This is Key Stage 3 science in the national curriculum for England. Pupils learn the particle model and diffusion in liquids and gases, driven by differences in concentration. They also meet Brownian motion in gases. They should explain diffusion with random particle motion. They should predict that it is faster in gases than in liquids, and faster when it is warmer.

Useful terms are particle, random motion, collision, concentration, concentration gradient, net movement, equilibrium and diffusion. The key word is net. Particles move both ways, and diffusion is the overall result. A bigger difference in concentration gives a faster net movement at first.

Common mistakes: thinking particles move on purpose towards the empty space, or that a draught is needed for a smell to spread. Many think particles stop once the spread is even. Pupils also mix up diffusion with dissolving or evaporating, or say it goes from low to high. A classic test uses ammonia and hydrogen chloride in a tube. The white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end, because the lighter ammonia particles move faster.

In the lab your child lifts a divider and watches purple particles spread with no push. They follow one particle's zigzag path and count crossings both ways until they balance. Then they race ink in water at two temperatures, and scent in air against ink in water. The lab speeds things up so you see it in seconds, but the order of the results is real.

familyTip: Drop a little food colouring into a glass of cold water and another of hot water without stirring. Which spreads first? Ask your child to explain it with moving particles.

visual.caption: Speeds diffusion up or slows it down? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: lift a divider and watch particles spread, follow one random path, count crossings at equilibrium, and race hot vs cold and gas vs liquid.

choices: The net movement of particles from high to low concentration
Particles moving from low to high concentration
A solid dissolving in a liquid
practice.hint: Think about where the particles end up: from crowded to less crowded.
practice.explain: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

practice.prompt: In 5 seconds, {a} scent particles cross the middle of a box from left to right and {b} cross from right to left. What is the net number that moved to the right?
practice.hint: Net means take the ones going back away from the ones going forward.
practice.explain: {a} right minus {b} left gives a net movement of {=a-b} particles to the right.

practice.prompt: Why does a single scent particle not head straight for the empty side of a room?
choices: It moves randomly and keeps colliding with other particles
It is attracted back to the bottle
Particles can only move up
practice.hint: Think about what happens to a particle each time it hits another one.
practice.explain: Each particle moves in a random direction and changes direction every time it collides, so its path zigzags.

practice.prompt: After diffusion is complete, each half of a box holds {k} dye particles. How many dye particles are in the whole box?
practice.hint: At equilibrium the two halves hold the same number.
practice.explain: Two halves of {k} each make {=2*k} particles in total.

pool.prompt: A drop of ink has spread evenly through a beaker of water. What are the ink particles doing?
choices: Still moving randomly, with no net movement
They have stopped moving
Moving to the bottom
pool.hint: Particles in a liquid never stop moving.
pool.explain: The particles keep moving, but as many go each way, so the concentration stays even and there is no net movement.

pool.prompt: In which will a smell spread fastest?
choices: Warm air
Cold air
Cold water
pool.hint: Gas beats liquid, and warmer beats colder.
pool.explain: Gas particles travel further between collisions than liquid particles, and warmer particles move faster, so warm air is fastest.

pool.prompt: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride gas diffuse from opposite ends of a glass tube. A white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end. Why?
choices: Ammonia particles are lighter, so they move faster
Hydrogen chloride particles are faster
The tube was tilted
pool.hint: The faster gas travels further before they meet.
pool.explain: Ammonia particles are lighter and move faster on average, so they travel further and meet the hydrogen chloride nearer its end.

pool.prompt: Ben says a fan is needed for perfume to spread across a room. What is right?
choices: It spreads anyway, by random particle motion
Ben is right, it cannot spread in still air
It only spreads if the room is hot
pool.hint: Think about the lab with no push at all.
pool.explain: Air currents can speed it up, but diffusion alone spreads the perfume, because the particles move randomly all the time.

pool.prompt: A tube is split into {n} equal sections. At equilibrium each section holds {k} gas particles. How many particles are in the tube?
pool.hint: At equilibrium every section holds the same number.

pool.prompt: Which is NOT an example of diffusion?
choices: Water boiling in a kettle
A smell of toast spreading through a house
Squash colour spreading through water without stirring
pool.hint: One of these is a change of state.
pool.explain: Boiling is a change of state from liquid to gas. The other two are particles spreading from high to low concentration.

pool.prompt: Why does ink spread more slowly in water than a smell spreads in air?
choices: Liquid particles are close together and collide more often
Liquid particles do not move
Ink particles are attracted to the glass
pool.hint: Think about how far a particle travels between bumps.
pool.explain: In a liquid the particles are packed close, so each one collides very often and travels only a short way between collisions.

pool.prompt: At equilibrium, in 10 seconds {a} particles cross a line from left to right. About how many cross from right to left in the same time?
pool.hint: At equilibrium there is no net movement.
pool.explain: No net movement means the crossings balance, so about {a} cross back the other way.
